title: Vivekananda (Chicago 1893
hook: a frog who has never left his well meets a frog from the sea

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vivekananda read out the Upanishad's call in Chicago: hear, children of immortal bliss. Did you try on that name? Day nine hundred forty-one.

A frog lives at the bottom of a well. He was born there, and he's done well for himself: he's fat, he's healthy, and he keeps the water clean of worms and bugs. One day another frog falls in. This one comes from the sea. The well frog is curious, and a little suspicious. Where are you from? The sea. And how big is the sea? Vivekananda told this story in Chicago, a few days into the Parliament, after speakers had been disagreeing. Today, why he answered an argument with a frog.
screen: `A FROG IN A WELL.` → `A FROG FROM THE SEA FALLS IN.` → `HOW BIG IS THE SEA?`

segments.voice: In his short talk called Why We Disagree, Vivekananda lets the story play out. Is the sea as big as my well? the frog asks, and he leaps from one side of the well to the other. Bigger, says the sea frog. The well frog takes a bigger leap. This big? Much bigger. You can't compare the sea with your well. And the well frog decides the visitor must be lying. Nothing can be bigger than my well, he says. Throw him out. Here's the turn. Vivekananda doesn't point the story at any one group in the hall. He puts himself in the story first: he's a Hindu, he says, sitting in his own little well and thinking the whole world is that well. Then he names the others the same way. Each of us, he says, is sitting in a little well and taking it for the world. He even thanks his American hosts for trying to break down the walls of those little worlds. That's the gentleness in it. The joke isn't on the frog for living in a well. Everyone has to live somewhere, and the well frog keeps his water clean. The trouble starts only at one sentence: nothing can be bigger than my well. It's a short talk, and he tells it like a joke, but it carries the same hope as his greeting days before. Not that anyone leaves home, but that people stop throwing out every visitor who says the water goes farther than they've seen.
screen: `THE FROG LEAPS ACROSS HIS WELL.` · `THROW HIM OUT, HE'S LYING.` · `"I'M SITTING IN MY OWN WELL."` · `EVERYONE HAS A WELL.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind your own well: the neighborhood, the family, the group or the way of seeing things you grew up inside. Notice what's good about it, the water you keep clean. Then remember one time someone told you the world was bigger than that, and you didn't want to hear it. No judging yourself. Just notice the leap the frog makes, measuring the sea against the walls. Breathe there for a while. The bell holds the time.
Vivekananda. The monk who told the Chicago Parliament he was a frog in his own well, too.
Your line: Vivekananda (Chicago 1893. Today, when someone says the water goes farther than you've seen, ask one more question before you decide they're wrong. Day nine hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Vivekananda's frog in the well is retold in Hindu talks, interfaith gatherings and school lessons as a picture of a narrow view, with the speaker himself counted among the frogs.

original.note: Sanskrit: the frog in the well, a saying for someone who takes their small world for the whole.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fable about a silly frog.
what it means: each of us takes our own little world for the whole one, and throws out whoever says otherwise.
what a scholar hears: Vivekananda turned the frog-in-the-well image, kupamanduka in Sanskrit, on every group in the hall, starting with himself.

sources.ref: Swami Vivekananda, Why We Disagree, World's Parliament of Religions, Chicago
sources.work: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda, vol. 1 (paraphrased)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the story's details in Why We Disagree (the well frog keeping the water clean of worms and bacilli, the leaps, 'throw him out', Vivekananda naming himself as a Hindu in his well, then Christians and Muslims in theirs, and thanking America for trying to break the barriers).
The voice says he 'names the others the same way' without listing them, to avoid any sense of ranking; a Keeper may prefer his own list.

Original: कूपमण्डूक (kūpamaṇḍūka), a traditional Sanskrit expression; confirm spelling and that the trapdoor's link between the Sanskrit idiom and his story is fairly put (he told it in English and did not name the idiom).
Date of the talk omitted under the claims rule ('a few days into the Parliament').
Editor pass: 'thanks the Parliament' changed to 'thanks his American hosts', matching the talk's thanks to America for trying to break the barriers.
